title: Thousands Celebrate Indian Culture at Oklahoma City's Food and Arts Festival
excerpt: The India Association of Oklahoma's annual festival brought regional cuisine, dance, fashion and hands-on craft traditions to Scissortail Park on Sunday, drawing one of the state's largest crowds for Indian culture.
body:
• The India Association of Oklahoma hosted its annual India Food and Arts Festival at Scissortail Park in Oklahoma City on Sunday.
  • The free festival featured authentic Indian cuisine, Bollywood and classical dance, an ethnic fashion show, live music and hands-on craft stations.
  • Organizers projected more than 16,000 visitors, making it one of Oklahoma's largest celebrations of Indian culture.
  • Vendor revenue and fees support IAOK's year-round educational initiatives and local small businesses across the state.

Thousands of visitors filled Scissortail Park on Sunday for the India Food and Arts Festival, the India Association of Oklahoma's flagship annual celebration of Indian culture — an event that has grown into one of the largest of its kind in the state.

The free, open-to-the-public festival packed the downtown park with a program built around three pillars: food, performance and hands-on craft. Attendees sampled regional Indian cuisine from vendors representing the country's diverse culinary traditions, watched stage performances spanning Bollywood numbers, folk dances and classical temple dances, and took part in interactive stations offering saree and turban tying, traditional henna art and Indian cooking demonstrations.

A stage full of Oklahoma talent

Much of the day's programming showcased local performers. Among the acts photographed at this year's event was a solo dance by Sakshi Kuwar, and a set by the Little Movers, a youth dance group led by Niharika Bharatha — a reminder that the festival doubles as a platform for Oklahoma's Indian dance academies and young artists.

The performance lineup also included an ethnic fashion show and live musical acts, while the festival's Artists Zone invited guests to try their hand at traditional crafts and learn about regional art forms. Clothing and jewelry vendors drew steady crowds, selling pieces from across India's many regions.

The organization behind it

The India Association of Oklahoma (IAOK), the nonprofit behind the festival, has staged the event for years as both a cultural showcase and a community bridge. In recent years it has drawn more than 16,000 attendees annually, according to organizers, earning its billing as one of Oklahoma's largest Indian cultural celebrations.

IAOK's stated mission is for people to enjoy and learn about India — and, in the words of association spokesperson Angela Oommen, "to let everyone know that we're all one and Oklahomans."

"To let everyone know that we're all one and Oklahomans."

— Angela Oommen, IAOK spokesperson

Earlier editions offered a taste of the festival's range: a menu that included dosa, chicken biryani, chole and mango lassi, alongside dance workshops, games including cricket, and opportunities for visitors to dress in traditional clothing. That family-friendly formula has carried through to this year's festival.

Why it matters

Beyond the cultural program, the festival serves an economic and educational purpose. Vendor participation gives local small businesses — many of them Indian American-owned restaurants, caterers and artisans — direct access to one of the year's biggest crowds, and proceeds support IAOK's year-round educational initiatives across Oklahoma, from school programs to community workshops.

For Oklahoma's Indian diaspora, the festival is also a moment of public visibility: a day when the community's food, music and craft take over one of Oklahoma City's most prominent public parks, and thousands of non-Indian Oklahomans show up to take part.

What's next

The festival returns each year, and IAOK uses the gathering to anchor its ongoing calendar of educational and cultural programming. For attendees who discovered the association on Sunday, the group's year-round workshops and events offer a way to stay connected long after the park empties out.
